content_list.content_text: Hollywood profited greatly from World War II. Besides proving itself an efficient wartime propaganda machine, the major studios successfully exported their products to the Allied countries, where filmmaking budgets were limited by the war effort.

Hollywood still seemed healthy in the years immediately after the war: 1946 was the year of highest movie attendance, beating the record set in 1939. The year's most successful film was Disney's Song of the South (1946), but the year's supposedly most important release was The Best Years of Our Lives (1946), by William Wyler (1902-1981).

information.contentText: John Fawell observes, in Dennis Perry's book Hitchcock and Poe: The Legacy of Delight and Terror, that Hitchcock "recognized that the darker side of voyeurism... is our desire for terrible things to happen to people... to make us feel better and relieve us of the burden of examining our own lives". The Master of Suspense challenges the audience, forcing them to peer through his rear window and expose themselves, as Donald Spoto put it in his 1976 book The Art of Alfred Hitchcock: Fifty Years of His Motion Pictures, to the "social contagion" of acting as voyeurs.

content_list.content_text: A drama about the return of three war veterans, the film addresses the complexity of the men's lives, the memories of combat that haunted them and the challenges their families and friends had to face. It ends on a relatively melancholy note, but there is no escaping the difficulties each of the characters will have to face, reflecting the sense of unease that pervaded much of the United States.

This ambivalence was present even in Frank Capra's (1897-1991) postwar classic It's a Wonderful Life (1946). The ending may show traces of the sentimentality that marred many of the director's films, but there is no doubt that a dark tone prevails throughout the film, especially in the intimidating performance of James Stewart (1908-1997). After serving in the U.S. Air Force, Stewart had to be persuaded to return to the movies.

information.contentTitle: Final scenes from It's a Wonderful Life (1946)
information.contentText: George is reunited with his family, his friends and his life – and a bell confirms that Clarence has earned his wings. An ending with a religious tone was proposed and then rejected, but the emotional impact of family and friends arriving to rescue George endures. Despite performing poorly at the box office due to stiff competition at the time of its release, the film became a classic and is a Christmas television staple around the world.

content_list.content_text: His experience on the battlefield had affected him deeply, which is reflected in the darker roles he went on to play. This change in his persona would be explored by Alfred Hitchcock (1899-1980) in Rear Window (1954) and Vertigo (1958), and by Anthony Mann (1906-1967), under whose direction he reached the peak of his career playing a number of morally compromised characters.

quote.quote: We didn't need dialogue. We had faces!
quote.author: Norma (Gloria Swanson) in Sunset Boulevard

content_list.content_text: The mix of light and shadow in actors, characters and films was exemplified by the work of Billy Wilder (1906-2002). One of cinema's most versatile directors, he was highly prolific in the 1940s and 1950s, alternating between the drama of The Lost Weekend (1945), the melancholy Sunset Boulevard (1950) and the creation of an icon named Marilyn Monroe (1926-1962) in The Seven Year Itch (1955) and Some Like It Hot (1959).

information.contentText: Acclaimed by many critics when it was released, Sunset Boulevard was nominated for eleven Oscars, winning three. It is widely accepted as a classic, often cited as one of the most remarkable films in American cinema. Deemed "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" by the U.S. Library of Congress in 1989, Sunset Boulevard was included in the first group of films selected for preservation in the National Film Registry. In 1998, it was named the twelfth greatest American film of all time on the list compiled by the American Film Institute. In 2007, in the updated edition of the list, it came in sixteenth.

content_list.content_text: Hollywood's shift toward darker territory had begun earlier, with the arrival of the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) in 1947. The committee was charged with investigating the infiltration of communist sympathizers among the film elite and, as a result, more than 250 members of the Hollywood community were barred from working in film, while many others were forced to name communists.

One of the most famous informers was Elia Kazan (1909-2003), whose film On the Waterfront (1954) seems like a response to his critics, with a mob informer (played by Marlon Brando) as its protagonist. Unlike Kazan, Ring Lardner Jr. (1915-2000), one of the many blacklisted screenwriters, cited for contempt during his 1947 testimony, told the committee: "I could answer the question (...) but if I did, I would hate myself in the morning." Writer Lillian Hellman was more incisive. In 1948, she wrote: "Naturally, men frightened to make pictures about the American Negro, men who only in the last year allowed the word Jew to be spoken in a picture, who took more than ten years to make an anti-fascist picture, these are frightened men and you pick frightened men to frighten first. Judas goats, they lead the others to the slaughter for you".

information.contentTitle: The famous scene from The Seven Year Itch (1955) with Marilyn Monroe
information.contentText: The Seven Year Itch became one of Fox's highest-grossing films of 1955 and cemented Marilyn Monroe's name as the biggest movie star and sex symbol of the era. The scene in which Marilyn's white dress is blown up on the street by the blast from a subway grate in the sidewalk became an icon of world cinema. The dress was auctioned in June 2011 for 5.6 million dollars.

content_list.content_text: Hollywood was terrified by the investigations, which cast a shadow over the industry. In a submissive reaction, several studios produced anticommunist films, among them My Son John (1952) and Pickup on South Street (1953). Even children's films, such as the adaptation The 5,000 Fingers of Dr. T. (1953), based on a book by Dr. Seuss, were considered to have communist connotations. The fad passed, but the damage caused by the investigations, along with the ever-growing hole in the studios' coffers, the impact of television and a more diverse audience less interested in what the studios had to offer, marked the end of the golden age of the Hollywood studios.

Although audiences packed movie theaters in the years immediately after the war, ticket sales began to decline in the late 1940s. During the war, people who stayed at home had more free time, and going to the movies was an efficient, fun and cheap way to keep busy.

quote.quote: From out of this sea of celluloid... William Wyler has fished a cinematic whale
quote.author: Time on Ben-Hur (1959)

content_list.content_text: But with the return of the veterans, people became busier with domestic life. The growth of the suburbs, the routine of looking for work and starting to support families were more important. In many cases, because of the postwar recession and the lack of jobs, a movie ticket was considered too expensive.

information.contentText: The film had the largest budget and the largest sets built in the history of cinema up to that time. Costume designer Elizabeth Haffenden oversaw a team of more than a hundred costume makers, with more than two hundred artists and workers working on the hundreds of friezes created for the production. Filming began on May 18, 1958, and wrapped on January 7, 1959, with shooting six days a week for twelve to fourteen hours a day. MGM executives made the decision to shoot Ben-Hur in widescreen format, a decision Wyler disliked. More than two hundred camels, 2,500 horses and ten thousand extras were used during filming. Post-production lasted six months, with the sea battle created using miniatures in a large water tank at MGM's studios in Culver City. The nine-minute chariot race became one of the most famous sequences in cinema, while the score composed by Miklós Rózsa is the longest ever composed and greatly influenced other epic films for more than fifteen years.

content_list.content_text: Television was a cheap form of entertainment. In 1940, there were 3,785 television sets in the United States. By 1960, nine out of 10 homes had a television. After the initial investment, these sets gave families endless hours of entertainment. Recognizing that audiences still loved the movies, the television networks began to compete with the studios, creating series that copied Hollywood's most popular genres. Success came so quickly that smaller studios went bankrupt and the networks bought up their properties and used them to film their own mass entertainment products.

content_list.title: Epics on the Screen
content_list.description:
A remake of a silent epic released in 1925, Ben-Hur was part of a series of spectacular films that were huge box office hits in the 1950s. After Quo Vadis (1951), The Robe (1953) and The Ten Commandments (1956), Ben-Hur was hailed as the greatest epic of all epics. But it is also remembered for a sarcastic quip ("Loved Ben. Hated Hur") as much as for its achievements. What prompted the criticism was that director William Wyler adopted the theory of Cecil B. DeMille (1881-1959) that audiences of biblical films allowed themselves to enjoy orgies and violence only because, in the end, divine wrath fell upon the wicked.

A more sophisticated filmmaker than DeMille, Wyler felt that it was not enough to bring the temple down on the villains. So the strong, simple story of Judah Ben-Hur (Charlton Heston), the noble Jew betrayed and enslaved by his false Roman friend Messala (Stephen Boyd), alternates crowd-pleasing action scenes with "inspirational" encounters with Christ, which allow Heston to deal with religious matters. Subsequent sword-and-sandal epics, from Spartacus (1960) to Gladiator (2000), toned down the preaching and turned up the violence, suggesting that a lesson had been learned. Still, while Heston and Boyd shine on their chariots, audiences can't help loving Ben-Hur. The film was the biggest commercial hit of the year and held the record for Oscars until Titanic (1997).

content_list.content_text: In response to this situation, the Hollywood studios began to explore areas where television could not compete. Thus epic films came into fashion for the first time since the silent era. Quo Vadis? (1951), The Robe (1953) and Salome (1953), The Ten Commandments (1956), Alexander the Great (1956) and Ben-Hur (1959) offered audiences large-scale spectacle. CinemaScope was created and theaters were modified to accommodate bigger screens. Other gimmicks, from 3D cinema to sensory devices that sprayed scents at the audience or gave small shocks through the seats, were also employed.

information.contentText: The parting of the Red Sea was considered the most difficult special effect ever achieved up to that time. The effect took about six months to complete in VistaVision. Two separately filmed scenes were combined: one on the shores of the Red Sea in Egypt, and the other at Paramount Studios in Hollywood, with a huge water tank split by a U-shaped trough, into which roughly 360,000 gallons of water were released from the sides. A giant waterfall, also built at Paramount, was filmed as well to create the effect of the walls of the sea parting in the middle.

content_list.content_text: More traditional genres were combined to satisfy audiences by offering something new. Thus family dramas were blended with Western elements in Giant (1956), the portrait of a family in the Texas oil fields directed by George Stevens (1904-1975). Douglas Sirk (1900-1987) followed the same path. With his expressionist colors used to grand effect in Magnificent Obsession (1954).

All That Heaven Allows (1955) and Imitation of Life (1959), and pushing the limits of what was permitted in terms of sexual content in the cinema of the time, his films offered a counterpoint to the mild tones of television dramas. But these fads attracted audiences only briefly, whereas TV series were able to secure viewers in the long run. Television quickly became the dominant form of entertainment for the American public. Hollywood's decline was hastened by legal changes to the studio system and by the work of foreign filmmakers.

information.contentText: A consummate example of melodrama, Magnificent Obsession, described in some quarters as "possibly Douglas Sirk's masterpiece" but also called "extravagant" and "ridiculous" by others, is the first in a series of hits the director achieved in the 1950s, produced by Ross Hunter or Albert S. Zugsmith, all at Universal Pictures.

content_list.content_text: The 1948 antitrust case - United States v. Paramount Pictures, Inc., 334 US 131 - put an end to years of vertical integration, under which the studios could own the theaters where their films were shown. The ruling also restricted block booking and the fixing of ticket prices. The impact of the decision shook Hollywood, wrecking a system that had prevailed for three decades. The new rules did significant damage to the increasingly empty coffers of this film district.

On top of that, there was bad news from abroad. War-ravaged countries saw cinema as a way to rebuild national pride, and nations such as France, Italy and the United Kingdom began producing their own films and stemming the flood of imports from the United States by imposing tariffs and quotas on them.

On the other hand, the end of film censorship gave filmmakers more freedom of expression in the United States. In 1952, the Supreme Court overturned a 1915 ruling, finally granting films the protection of free speech guaranteed by the First Amendment. The law also allowed individuals to challenge decisions made by censorship boards, and that is what Otto Preminger (1905-1986) did in 1953, when Kansas, Ohio and Maryland tried to ban his film The Moon Is Blue (1953) for the audacity of using the word virgin.

information.contentText: This is one of several Hitchcock films featuring a score by Bernard Herrmann and an opening title sequence by graphic designer Saul Bass, which is often cited as the first in film history to make extended use of kinetic typography.

content_list.content_text: Questions of responsibility and social rights were also raised in 12 Angry Men (1957), directed by Sidney Lumet (b. 1924). Besides being a tight drama with excellent performances, the film confronts prejudice and stirs the collective conscience three years before the start of a new era of social revolution.

The world and cinema were about to change. The rebellious teenagers of the 1950s became the bikers of the 1960s; the fun-loving hero of many screwball comedies, Cary Grant (1904-1986), was fighting to save himself in North by Northwest (1959); handsome Tony Curtis (1925-2010) subverted his image in 1957 by playing press agent Sidney Falco in the noir-tinged Sweet Smell of Success (1957); American directors were beginning to be influenced by French directors; and, in reaction to social and political upheaval, a new era of cinematic violence and liberal productions was about to take shape. Hollywood's golden age was over, and cinema awaited its bold and uncertain future.

movies.title: Rear Window
movies.overview: A wheelchair-bound photographer spies on his neighbors from his apartment window and becomes convinced one of them has committed murder.

movies.title: Ben-Hur
movies.overview: Judah Ben-Hur, a Palestinian Jew, is battling the Roman empire at the time of Christ. His actions send him and his family into slavery, but an inspirational encounter with Jesus changes everything. He finally meets his rival in a justly famous chariot race and rescues his suffering family.

movies.title: The Seven Year Itch
movies.overview: With his family away for their annual summer holiday, Richard Sherman decides he has the opportunity to live a bachelor's life. The beautiful but ditzy blonde from the apartment above catches his eye and they soon start spending time together—maybe a little too much time!

movies.title: Vertigo
movies.overview: A retired San Francisco detective suffering from acrophobia investigates the strange activities of an old friend's wife, all the while becoming dangerously obsessed with her.

movies.title: The Ten Commandments
movies.overview: Escaping death, a Hebrew infant is raised in a royal household to become a prince. Upon discovery of his true heritage, Moses embarks on a personal quest to reclaim his destiny as the leader and liberator of the Hebrew people.

movies.title: It's a Wonderful Life
movies.overview: A holiday favourite for generations...  George Bailey has spent his entire life giving to the people of Bedford Falls.  All that prevents rich skinflint Mr. Potter from taking over the entire town is George's modest building and loan company.  But on Christmas Eve the business's $8,000 is lost and George's troubles begin.

movies.title: Some Like It Hot
movies.overview: Two musicians witness a mob hit and struggle to find a way out of the city before they are found by the gangsters. Their only opportunity is to join an all-girl band as they leave on a tour. To make their getaway they must first disguise themselves as women, then keep their identities secret and deal with the problems this brings - such as an attractive bandmate and a very determined suitor.

movies.title: North by Northwest
movies.overview: Advertising man Roger Thornhill is mistaken for a spy, triggering a deadly cross-country chase.

content_list.subtitle: The events that shaped the world
content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1940 to 1959
content_list.description: Asian cinema gains even more prominence with the release of several masterpieces. Film noir emerges and musicals continue to shine on the big screen. The Western holds on to its reign as one of the most popular genres, and one of the most important movements in cinema takes place in France: the French New Wave.
